title: What human factors and continuation training must a CASA Part 145 maintenance organization provide?
description: CASR Part 145 MOS explained: human factors understanding, continuation training every 24 months, certifying staff authorizations, experience and records.
shortAnswer: Under the Part 145 Manual of Standards made under the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998, an Australian approved maintenance organization must ensure staff understand human factors relevant to their role, keep everyone who performs maintenance up to date on technology, procedures and human factors principles, and run a continuation training program in its exposition: training before a person certifies for maintenance and at least once every 24 months afterward. Certification authorizations last no more than 2 years.
keyTakeaways: Section 145.A.30(e) of the Part 145 Manual of Standards requires competence standards in the exposition and an understanding of human factors and human performance issues appropriate to each person's function.
Section 145.A.35(e) requires a continuation training program: training before certifying for the organization and at least once every 24 months after starting maintenance work for it.

Certifying staff need at least 6 months of relevant maintenance experience in any preceding 2 year period, and each certification authorization may remain in force for a maximum of 2 years (145.A.35(b) and (c)).
Records of certifying employees, including training history with the organization, are kept for at least 2 years after the person stops holding an authorization (145.A.35(j)).
Part 145 organizations must also have a drug and alcohol management plan with its own education program under CASR Part 99.
regulator: Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA), under Part 145 of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998 and the Part 145 Manual of Standards
appliesTo: Part 145 approved maintenance organizations (AMOs) providing aircraft and aeronautical product maintenance
Certifying employees, including Part 66 licensed engineers and specialist maintenance certifying staff
All employees who perform maintenance services on behalf of the AMO
Quality managers and others who issue and revoke certification authorizations

sections.heading: Where do Part 145 training requirements come from?

blocks.text: The training detail is in the Part 145 Manual of Standards (MOS), made under regulations 145.005 and 145.015 of the [Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F1998B00220/latest/text). As at November 2026 the Federal Register of Legislation shows the [Part 145 Manual of Standards](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2011L00281/latest/text) as in force, with the compilation of March 18, 2015 (F2015C00263) as its latest version.

The MOS works through the approved maintenance organization's exposition. Many obligations are framed as "the AMO must have in its exposition" a standard, program or procedure, which means CASA audits both what the exposition says and whether the organization does it. CASA's own [guidance on Part 145 organizations](https://www.casa.gov.au/aircraft/airworthiness/maintenance-organisations/requirements-approved-maintenance-organisations-part-145) states that its expectations are based on the Part 145 MOS.

sections.heading: What does Part 145 require on human factors?

blocks.text: Human factors appears in three places in the MOS: individual understanding, up to date knowledge, and the organization's maintenance procedures. The MOS defines human factors principles as "principles that deal with the interaction between human performance and maintenance system components that are applied to improve safety of air navigation."

blocks.text: The scope of 145.A.30(e) is notably wider than certifying staff. Planners, stores staff with maintenance roles, managers and quality auditors all fall within "any maintenance, management or quality audit task", so a human factors program limited to licensed engineers leaves a gap. A [training needs analysis](/guides/how-to-conduct-a-training-needs-analysis) by function is the usual way to set the level appropriate to each role.

sections.heading: How often is continuation training required?

blocks.text: Continuation training is required before a person certifies for maintenance on behalf of the AMO and at least once every 24 months after they start performing maintenance services for it. Section 145.A.35(e) requires the program to be set out in the exposition.

The MOS does not prescribe a syllabus or minimum hours. Read together with 145.A.35(d), the content should keep employees current on the three named areas: technology relevant to their functions, the AMO's procedures, and human factors principles. In practice that means continuation training should change from cycle to cycle as procedures, fleet types and occurrence findings change.

blocks.title: Linking to error reporting
blocks.text: Section 145.A.65(a) requires safety and quality policies that encourage employees to report maintenance related incidents and errors. Feeding de-identified findings from those reports into the next continuation training cycle is a practical way to show that human factors training reflects the organization's own risks.

sections.heading: What extra requirements apply to certifying staff?

blocks.text: Certifying staff must be assessed, experienced and authorized for a defined scope, with the authorization limited to 2 years. Section 145.A.35 sets the conditions.

items: **Understanding before issue:** before issuing or reissuing an authorization, the AMO must ensure the employee understands the relevant aircraft or products and the AMO's procedures and exposition (145.A.35(a)).
**Assessment:** the AMO must assess competence, qualification and capability under an exposition procedure before issue or reissue (145.A.35(f)).
**Duration:** an authorization may remain in force for a maximum of 2 years and only while the holder keeps the qualification it was based on (145.A.35(b)).
**Recent experience:** at least 6 months of relevant maintenance experience in any preceding 2 year period (145.A.35(c)).
**Minimum age:** no authorization to anyone under 21 (145.A.35(m)).
**Written scope:** the employee receives written details of scope, limitations, issue and expiry dates and a reference number (145.A.35(h)).

blocks.text: Category A license holders may certify on a specific type only after task training that includes practical and theoretical elements, demonstrated by an examination or workplace assessment (145.A.35(n)). Where an AMO provides permitted type training under 145.A.37, it may issue an authorization once only, for 6 months, and must issue a notice of completion in the CASA approved form. For assessment design, see [how to set up verification of competency](/guides/how-to-set-up-verification-of-competency).

sections.heading: What training records must a Part 145 organization keep?

blocks.text: The AMO must keep a record of all certifying employees, including their training history with the AMO, and retain it securely for at least 2 years after the employee stops holding an authorization. Section 145.A.35(j) also requires the record to include each authorization's number, scope and limitations, and the employee's license, qualification and experience details.

items: On request, the AMO must give a certifying employee a copy of the records held about them (145.A.35(j)(3)).
Certifying employees must have access to their authorization in documented or electronic form (145.A.35(k)).
The AMO or certifying employee must produce copies of an authorization to a CASA authorized person within 24 hours of a request (145.A.35(l)).

blocks.text: The 24 hour production rule is the practical test of a records system: authorizations, training history and expiry dates need to be retrievable quickly, not reconstructed from paper files. See [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines human factors principles, AMO procedures and type technology as separate knowledge areas mapped to each function in the exposition, so each 24 month continuation cycle can target what changed and each authorization reissue can draw on evidence of what the person actually demonstrated.

faqs.q: Is Part 145 continuation training required every two years?
faqs.a: At least every 24 months. Section 145.A.35(e) of the Part 145 Manual of Standards requires training before a person certifies for maintenance on behalf of the AMO and at least once every 24 months after they start performing maintenance services for it. An AMO may choose a shorter cycle in its exposition.

faqs.q: Does continuation training apply only to licensed engineers?
faqs.a: No. Section 145.A.35(e) applies to employees who perform maintenance services on behalf of the AMO, and 145.A.30(e) requires human factors understanding from everyone involved in maintenance, management or quality audit tasks. Licensed certifying staff have additional authorization, assessment and experience requirements.

faqs.q: Does the Part 145 MOS set a human factors syllabus?
faqs.a: No. The MOS requires an understanding appropriate to each function and up to date knowledge of human factors principles, but does not set a syllabus or hours. For staff qualified under a foreign license, Appendix III requires human factors training equivalent to that detailed in CASR Part 66.

faqs.q: Do Part 145 organizations need drug and alcohol training too?
faqs.a: Yes. Regulation 99.030 of CASR lists Part 145 organizations among those that must have a drug and alcohol management plan when staff perform safety sensitive aviation activities, and maintenance and certification are listed activities. The DAMP must include an education program for employees and DAMP supervisors.
